title: Diffraction & crystal structure
interaction: Place atoms in a unit cell and choose the lattice; the page builds the reciprocal lattice and lights up each Bragg reflection with its structure factor, so adding a second atom at the body centre makes half the spots vanish. Rotate the crystal in a monochromatic beam to see which reflections flash, then load a real structure (salt, diamond, quartz) from the Crystallography Open Database and compare its computed powder pattern with the cell you built.
takeaway: A diffraction pattern is the crystal's lattice seen in reciprocal space, and the brightness of each spot encodes where the atoms sit within the cell.
needs: Crystal structures as CIF files from the Crystallography Open Database; CC0.
pitfall: Diffraction does not image atoms: the spots give the Fourier transform's magnitudes and the phases are lost, which is why a structure must be inferred.
why: MIT OCW 8.231 Physics of Solids I: diffraction and the reciprocal lattice, Bloch's theorem: https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/8-231-physics-of-solids-i-fall-2006/pages/syllabus/
overlapWith: semiconductors: shows lattices beside energy bands; this page is how the lattices are known at all, from their diffraction patterns.
needsSource: Crystallography Open Database, https://www.crystallography.net/cod/ ; CC0 with a request to cite the original authors.

title: The Dirac equation
interaction: Launch a wave packet governed by the one-dimensional Dirac equation and watch its two spinor components: at low momentum it moves like a Schrödinger packet, near c it respects the speed limit and trembles (Zitterbewegung) when positive- and negative-energy parts mix. Raise a potential step above twice the rest energy and the packet passes through where Schrödinger says it must stop (the Klein paradox), the first sign of antiparticles.
takeaway: Marrying quantum mechanics to special relativity forces a second set of solutions on the equation, and they are the antiparticles.
pitfall: Negative-energy states are not negative mass or an error; present them as the positron's states.
why: MIT OCW 8.323 Relativistic Quantum Field Theory I: Dirac theory: https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/8-323-relativistic-quantum-field-theory-i-spring-2023/pages/syllabus
overlapWith: standard-model: lists the antiparticles; this page shows where they come from in the equation.

title: Feynman diagrams
interaction: Choose the incoming and outgoing particles of a QED process and draw diagrams from a palette of electron, muon and photon lines joined at vertices; the page checks each against the rules, grades it by its powers of the coupling, and evaluates the tree-level amplitude numerically to plot the angular distribution and the cross section against energy. Compare electron-positron annihilation into muon pairs with the LEP measurements.
takeaway: Each diagram is a term in a calculation, its vertices count the powers of a small number, and summing the few lowest ones reproduces what colliders measure.
needs: Measured e+e- → μ+μ- cross sections and asymmetries from LEP at 192-208 GeV, HEPData record 48691 and its companions, released under CC0.
pitfall: Diagrams are not pictures of what happens: the virtual photon is a term in a sum, and the page must not animate it as a real particle in flight.
why: MIT OCW 8.323 Relativistic Quantum Field Theory I: Feynman diagrams, Feynman rules and e+e- → μ+μ-: https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/8-323-relativistic-quantum-field-theory-i-spring-2023/pages/syllabus
overlapWith: standard-model: steps through beta decay as an exchange of force carriers; this page turns the diagram into a calculator whose output is compared with collider data.
needsSource: HEPData (CERN), https://www.hepdata.net/record/48691; terms of use say datasets are CC0 unless stated otherwise, https://hepdata.net/terms

title: Magnetohydrodynamics: frozen-in field lines
interaction: Paint a flow (a vortex, a shear, a converging stream) over a conducting fluid threaded by a magnetic field and set the magnetic Reynolds number: the page integrates the induction equation on a grid, and the field lines are swept, stretched and wound up with the fluid at high values, or slip through it and diffuse away at low ones. Pluck a field line and watch an Alfvén wave run along it.
takeaway: In a good conductor the magnetic field is carried with the fluid like dye, so moving the fluid stretches and winds the field, which is how stars and planets build theirs.
pitfall: Field lines moving with the fluid is a theorem about ideal conductors, not a property of magnetic fields in general; show the diffusive case beside it.
why: MIT OCW 22.611J Introduction to Plasma Physics I: MHD models, equilibrium and stability: https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/22-611j-introduction-to-plasma-physics-i-fall-2003/pages/syllabus
overlapWith: nuclear-fusion: holds a plasma in a magnetic bottle; this page shows the field being moved by the conducting fluid instead of the other way round.

title: Hamiltonian mechanics & phase space
interaction: Pan and zoom the phase portrait of a pendulum and hover to launch a trajectory, finding the separatrix between swinging and spinning. Drop a cloud of nearby starting states and watch it stretch and fold while its area stays exactly fixed; add friction and the area shrinks toward a point. Switch to a periodically kicked rotor and scrub the kick strength to see its Poincaré section go from nested curves to a chaotic sea.
takeaway: Hamiltonian flow moves a cloud of states through phase space like an incompressible fluid, preserving its area, and only dissipation can shrink it.
pitfall: Area preservation does not mean the cloud keeps its shape: it stretches into filaments that look like they fill the space, which is where coarse-grained entropy comes from.
why: MIT OCW 8.223 Classical Mechanics II, lectures 15-19 on Hamiltonian mechanics and Poisson brackets: https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/8-223-classical-mechanics-ii-january-iap-2017/pages/syllabus
overlapWith: chaos-fractals: starts two double pendulums and zooms the Mandelbrot set; this page is about the geometry of the state space itself, its conserved area and the Poincaré section.

title: The Schrödinger equation & the hydrogen atom
interaction: Shoot the radial Schrödinger equation numerically: slide the trial energy and watch the wavefunction blow up one way or the other until it settles into a bound state, then collect the ladder of levels and their 1/n² pattern. Pick n, l and m to render the orbital's probability cloud, and compare the computed Balmer wavelengths with the measured lines from the NIST database.
takeaway: Hydrogen's spectral lines are the differences between the only energies at which a wave fits around the proton, and the orbitals are the shapes of those fitted waves.
needs: Hydrogen energy levels and Balmer-line wavelengths from the NIST Atomic Spectra Database (SRD 78); US government data, public domain.
pitfall: The 1s state has zero angular momentum and is not a circular orbit; the cloud is a probability density, not a smeared-out electron.
why: MIT OCW 8.04 Quantum Physics I: Schrödinger's equation in three dimensions, central potentials and hydrogenic systems: https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/8-04-quantum-physics-i-spring-2013/pages/syllabus
overlapWith: atoms-periodic-table: fills shells and views orbital shapes in 3D; this page solves the equation that produces those shells and checks its energies against measured lines.
needsSource: NIST ASD, https://physics.nist.gov/asd; NIST data, public domain in the US under the NIST open licence.

title: The Ising model & phase transitions
interaction: Run a lattice of spins with the Metropolis algorithm and slide the temperature through the critical point: domains grow out of noise, the magnetization jumps from zero to nearly full, and the susceptibility and heat capacity spike. Apply a field and sweep it back and forth to trace a hysteresis loop; grow the lattice to see the transition sharpen, and shrink it to one dimension to see it vanish.
takeaway: Nearest-neighbour alignment alone produces a sharp phase transition, and the ordered state appears at a precise temperature only in the limit of a large system.
pitfall: A one-dimensional chain has no phase transition at any temperature above zero; show that case so the reader does not believe order is automatic.
why: MIT OCW RES.8-010 Introduction to Statistical Physics, lecture 8 on the Ising model via its partition function: https://www.ocw.mit.edu/courses/res-8-010-introduction-to-statistical-physics-summer-2018/mitres_8_010su18_lec8.pdf
overlapWith: states-of-matter: freezes and boils a box of molecules; this page strips a transition down to the simplest possible model and shows the critical point's divergences.

title: Synchronization: metronomes, bridges and the Kuramoto model
interaction: A hundred oscillators drawn as dots running round a circle, each with its own natural rate drawn from a bell curve, and a slider for how strongly each pulls on the others. Below a critical coupling the dots smear round the circle and the order parameter stays near zero; above it a clump forms and grows, with the locked fraction and the critical value plotted against the spread of rates. Load the real cases: metronomes on a board whose sway couples them, the Millennium Bridge whose walkers' steps locked once enough of them were on it (the published model and parameters), and a ring of neighbours-only coupling that locks into travelling waves instead.
takeaway: Oscillators that pull weakly on each other stay independent, but above a sharp coupling threshold a growing fraction locks together, so synchrony appears suddenly, in metronomes, fireflies and a wobbling bridge.
needs: Parameters for the Millennium Bridge case from Strogatz et al. 2005.
pitfall: Synchrony needs neither a leader nor identical oscillators; the spread of natural rates against the coupling decides. The Millennium Bridge wobble was sideways, driven by walkers' lateral steps locking to the sway, not by people marching in time.
why: Veritasium's 'The Surprising Secret of Synchronization' (2021), built on Strogatz's Sync, is one of the channel's most-watched: https://veritasium.com/videos/2021/3/31/the-secret-of-synchronization
overlapWith: oscillations-resonance: one oscillator driven at a frequency; this page is many self-sustained oscillators with their own rates locking to each other, a phase transition in the coupling. fireflies-in-sync (this batch, level 0) is the pulse-coupled toy.
needsSource: none for the base model; the bridge case uses the numbers published in Strogatz, Abrams, McRobie, Eckhardt & Ott, Nature 2005 (cited).

title: Lasers
interaction: Pump a four-level gain medium between two mirrors and watch the populations and the photon number evolve under the rate equations: below threshold the cavity holds a few spontaneous photons, and at threshold the inversion clamps while the output climbs linearly with pump power. Lower the mirror reflectivity, switch to a three-level or a two-level medium, or open and close a shutter to see relaxation oscillations and a Q-switched pulse.
takeaway: A laser is a cavity in which stimulated emission out-competes loss, and above that threshold every extra pumped atom adds a photon to the same mode.
pitfall: Population inversion is impossible by pumping a two-level system at any power; the page must show the two-level case saturating at equal populations.
why: PhET 'Lasers' is in its quantum collection, and MIT OCW 6.977 builds threshold and inversion from the rate equations: https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/6-977-semiconductor-optoelectronics-theory-and-design-fall-2002/
overlapWith: solar-cells: a junction turns photons into current; this is the inverse, a medium amplifying light, and the LED half of the Reserve item is a sentence in semiconductors, not a page.

title: The principle of least action
interaction: Drag the control points of a ball's path through a space-time plot between two fixed events; the action (kinetic minus potential energy summed along the path) is computed live and compared with the true trajectory, and the path snaps toward the stationary one when released. Switch the potential to a spring, a planet or a light ray crossing two media and watch the straight line, the ellipse and the refracted ray each fall out of the same rule.
takeaway: Nature's path between two events is the one whose action is stationary, and the laws of motion and refraction are that one rule in different potentials.
pitfall: The true path makes the action stationary, not always least: for a long enough path in a spring potential it is a saddle, and the page must show that case rather than call it a minimum.
why: MIT OCW 8.223 Classical Mechanics II, lectures 1-4 on Lagrangian mechanics with the reading 'When action is not least' (Gray & Taylor): https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/8-223-classical-mechanics-ii-january-iap-2017/pages/syllabus
overlapWith: newtons-laws: that page pushes carts with forces; this one derives the same motions from a single scalar quantity attached to a whole path.

title: Maxwell's equations on a grid
interaction: Draw metal walls, dielectric blocks and a current source on a grid; the page integrates Maxwell's two curl equations step by step (the Yee scheme) and paints the electric and magnetic fields as they evolve. Build a dipole antenna and see its radiation pattern, a waveguide that cuts off below a frequency, a slab that focuses a pulse.
takeaway: A changing electric field makes a magnetic field and vice versa, and iterating those two rules on a grid is enough to make antennas radiate, guides channel and lenses focus.
pitfall: The grid is not the physics: show the time-step limit (Courant condition) and the numerical dispersion so the reader does not take grid artefacts for wave behaviour.
why: MIT OCW 8.07 Electromagnetism II: Maxwell's equations, electromagnetic waves, radiation: https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/8-07-electromagnetism-ii-fall-2012/
overlapWith: electromagnetism: shows static field lines and induction in a coil; this page solves the full time-dependent equations on a grid so that waves, antennas and guides emerge from them.

title: Fluid flow & the Navier-Stokes equations
interaction: Drive a fluid past a cylinder (a lattice-Boltzmann solver on a grid) and slide the Reynolds number: at low values the flow creeps symmetrically around it, then a pair of standing eddies forms, then vortices shed alternately into a wavy street whose frequency the page measures, and finally the wake turns irregular. Draw your own obstacle, add a second one downstream, and watch the drag.
takeaway: One dimensionless number, the ratio of inertia to viscosity, decides whether a flow is smooth, periodic or turbulent, whatever the fluid or the size.
pitfall: Turbulence is not randomness injected into the model; it emerges from the deterministic equations at high Reynolds number and the page must not add noise.
why: MIT OCW 2.25 Advanced Fluid Mechanics: Navier-Stokes, similarity and dimensional analysis, boundary layers and separation: https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/2-25-advanced-fluid-mechanics-fall-2013/pages/syllabus
overlapWith: flight: puts a wing in a stream and shows lift and stall; this page is the governing equation itself, swept through Reynolds number to the onset of turbulence.

title: Noether's theorem
interaction: Run a simulated planet, a bead on a wire or two colliding masses, then apply a transformation to the whole experiment with a dial: shift it in space, rotate it, shift it in time. Meters show which of momentum, angular momentum and energy stays constant along the trajectory; break a symmetry by adding a wall, a fixed centre or a potential that changes with time and watch the matching meter start to drift while the others hold.
takeaway: Every continuous symmetry of a system's action comes paired with a quantity that stays constant, and breaking the symmetry is exactly what lets that quantity change.
pitfall: The symmetry belongs to the action, not to the motion: an elliptical orbit is not rotationally symmetric, yet angular momentum is conserved because the potential is.
why: MIT OCW 8.223 Classical Mechanics II, the lectures on conserved quantities that follow the Lagrangian unit: https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/8-223-classical-mechanics-ii-january-iap-2017/pages/syllabus
overlapWith: newtons-laws: shows energy and momentum conserved in collisions; here conservation is derived from a symmetry and switched off by breaking that symmetry.

title: The partition function
interaction: Build a small system from a palette of energy levels (a two-level atom, a quantum oscillator, a rotor, a particle in a box) and slide the temperature: the page computes the Boltzmann weights and their sum, the partition function, and fills each level with its share of the population. Linked plots show the mean energy and heat capacity; watch the Schottky bump of a two-level system and the freezing-out of an oscillator's heat capacity, then compare the oscillator model with the measured heat capacity of diamond.
takeaway: Once a system's energy levels are known, one sum over them fixes its energy, heat capacity and entropy at every temperature.
needs: Measured heat capacity of diamond against temperature as tabulated by Einstein (1907) from Weber's measurements; public domain.
pitfall: Temperature is not average energy: a two-level system's energy saturates, so its heat capacity rises and then falls back to zero as it gets hotter.
why: MIT OCW 8.044 Statistical Physics I: microcanonical and canonical ensembles: https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/8-044-statistical-physics-i-spring-2013/pages/syllabus
overlapWith: entropy: counts the microstates of a gas at fixed energy; this page fixes the temperature instead and shows how the Boltzmann weighting over levels yields every thermal property.
needsSource: Einstein, Annalen der Physik 22 (1907), table of Weber's diamond heat-capacity data; public domain.

title: Perturbation theory
interaction: Add a small extra term to a potential (an electric field on hydrogen, an x⁴ term on an oscillator) and slide its strength: the page diagonalizes the full problem numerically and lays the exact levels beside the first- and second-order estimates, so the reader sees where the series tracks and where it fails. Then switch the perturbation on and off in time and watch transitions appear at the rate Fermi's golden rule predicts.
takeaway: A problem you cannot solve can be approximated from one you can, order by order, and the exact answer tells you where the series stops tracking.
pitfall: The series for the anharmonic oscillator diverges for any coupling; show the terms getting worse past some order rather than implying convergence.
why: MIT OCW 8.06 Quantum Physics III: time-independent and time-dependent perturbation theory, Fermi's golden rule: https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/8-06-quantum-physics-iii-spring-2018/
overlapWith: hydrogen-atom: solves the unperturbed atom; this page adds a field to it and shows the Stark shifts and transitions that result.

title: Plasma: shielding, oscillations & Landau damping
interaction: Run a one-dimensional particle-in-cell plasma: drop in a test charge and watch electrons cloud around it until its field dies beyond the Debye length; displace a slab of electrons and release it to ring at the plasma frequency; launch a wave and see it fade as particles moving at its speed absorb it (Landau damping); send two beams through each other and watch the instability grow.
takeaway: A plasma shields, oscillates and trades energy with waves collectively, through its own electric field rather than through collisions.
pitfall: Landau damping takes energy from the wave with no collisions at all; do not add a friction term and call it damping.
why: MIT OCW 22.611J Introduction to Plasma Physics I: Debye shielding, plasma waves, Landau damping, streaming instabilities: https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/22-611j-introduction-to-plasma-physics-i-fall-2003/pages/syllabus
overlapWith: nuclear-fusion: confines a plasma as a hot fluid to reach ignition; this page is the plasma's own electrostatic behaviour, particle by particle.

title: Where the energy in a circuit really flows
interaction: A battery, two long wires and a lamp on a grid; the page solves for the surface charges on the wires held at their potentials, draws the electric field, the magnetic field of the current and the Poynting vector, the energy flow, as arrows in the space around the wires: it leaves the battery through the surrounding space, runs alongside the wires and dives into the lamp from outside, with almost none inside the metal. Drag the lamp away and the flow follows the wires; make the wires resistive and watch some energy dive into them along their length. Replay the thought experiment of a lamp a metre from a battery joined by wires a light-second long, run in the time domain, with a small transient reaching the lamp in nanoseconds and the full current only after the round trip.
takeaway: Electrical energy travels in the fields around the wires, not inside them: the Poynting vector flows from the battery through space into the lamp, and the wires only guide it.
pitfall: Energy flowing through space does not mean the lamp lights fully at once or that wires are unnecessary: the wires' surface charges guide the fields, and in the long-wire experiment only a small transient arrives early. The Poynting vector is a classical field quantity; nothing about electrons 'carrying' energy or not.
why: Veritasium's 'The Big Misconception About Electricity' (2021) drew tens of millions of views and months of engineering-forum argument: https://veritasium.com/videos/2021/11/19/the-big-misconception-about-electricity
overlapWith: electric-circuits: current and voltage in loops, whose pitfall already notes that charges drift slowly while the lamp lights at once; this page shows where the energy travels, in the fields outside the wires. maxwell-equations (pool) is a Yee grid for antennas and waveguides and could host the time-domain run; radiating-charge (pool) is one charge's field.

title: The quantum harmonic oscillator
interaction: Slide up the energy ladder of a quantum spring and see each level's wavefunction and probability density against the classical turning points. Mix levels with the raising operator to build a coherent state and press play: the packet swings back and forth like a classical mass without spreading, while a squeezed state breathes and a single level stands still.
takeaway: A quantum spring holds energy only in equal steps, and the right superposition of those steps moves exactly like the classical oscillator.
pitfall: The ground state has energy and its probability leaks past the classical turning points; the lowest state is not 'at rest'.
why: MIT OCW 8.05 Quantum Physics II course description: the harmonic oscillator, spin and angular momentum: https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/8-05-quantum-physics-ii-fall-2013/pages/syllabus
overlapWith: quantum-mechanics: sends a free packet at a barrier; this page confines the packet in a spring, the one potential whose quantum states underlie photons and phonons.

title: Quantum scattering
interaction: Fire a plane wave at a spherical well or barrier and set its energy and the well's depth: the page solves each partial wave's phase shift and draws the scattered wave, the angular pattern and the cross section against energy. Sweep the energy through a resonance and watch the cross section spike while a wave lingers inside the well; compare with the classical hard-sphere answer.
takeaway: What a beam scatters off a target tells you the target's shape and size, and resonances appear where a wave can momentarily fit inside.
pitfall: At low energy a quantum target's cross section can be four times its geometric area, not equal to it; do not draw the classical disc as the answer.
why: MIT OCW 8.06 Quantum Physics III: scattering, partial waves and phase shifts, the Born approximation: https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/8-06-quantum-physics-iii-spring-2018/
overlapWith: quantum-mechanics: a 1D packet hits a barrier; this page scatters in three dimensions and reads off cross sections, which is how particle and nuclear experiments see.

title: The field of a moving charge
interaction: Drag a charge around the stage, or set it to oscillate, orbit or stop dead; the page draws its electric field lines from the retarded time (Liénard-Wiechert), so a sudden stop sends a kink racing outward at the speed of light while the field inside is already the new one. Push the speed toward c and watch the field flatten into a pancake and the radiation beam forward.
takeaway: News of a charge's motion travels outward at c, and the kink where the old field meets the new one is the radiation.
pitfall: A charge moving at constant velocity does not radiate, however fast it goes; only acceleration makes a kink.
why: MIT OCW 8.07 Electromagnetism II: emission, absorption and scattering of radiation, relativistic electrodynamics: https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/8-07-electromagnetism-ii-fall-2012/
overlapWith: electromagnetism: places static charges and shows their field lines; here the charge moves and the field lines show retardation and radiation.

title: Renormalization: the same picture at every scale
interaction: Freeze a snapshot of the Ising lattice at a chosen temperature and coarse-grain it like a zoom-out: every 3×3 block is replaced by its majority spin, again and again. Below the critical temperature the picture flows to all-up, above it to pure noise, and right at the critical point it looks the same at every magnification. A dial plots the nearest-neighbour correlation of the blocked lattice after each step, and the flow has a single unstable fixed point.
takeaway: Coarse-graining drives a system toward one of a few fixed points, and the critical point is the one that looks the same at every scale, which is why unrelated materials share the same critical exponents.
pitfall: The majority-rule block spin is a heuristic, not an exact transformation; say that the exact 2D exponents come from Onsager and that the flow shown is Kadanoff's picture.
why: MIT OCW 8.334 Statistical Mechanics II: universality, the scaling hypothesis and Kadanoff's heuristic renormalization group: https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/8-334-statistical-mechanics-ii-statistical-physics-of-fields-spring-2014/
overlapWith: ising-model: runs the simulation and finds the transition; this page zooms out of its snapshots to show scale invariance and the flow of couplings.

title: Orbits in curved spacetime
interaction: Set a body's energy and angular momentum around a Schwarzschild mass; the page draws the relativistic effective potential beside the Newtonian one and integrates the geodesic: orbits precess, the innermost stable circular orbit appears at three Schwarzschild radii, and inside it the body spirals in. Dial the mass to the Sun's and the orbit to Mercury's to read off 43 arcseconds per century; spin the mass (Kerr) and watch orbits dragged around with it.
takeaway: General relativity adds one extra term to the orbital potential, and that term is what makes orbits precess and sets a closest stable orbit.
pitfall: Precession is not a Newtonian effect of a bigger mass: in a pure 1/r potential every orbit closes, and the page must show that beside the relativistic one.
why: MIT OCW 8.962 General Relativity: geodesic trajectories, symmetries and conserved quantities, black holes: https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/8-962-general-relativity-spring-2020/pages/syllabus
overlapWith: black-holes: fires rays and probes past a hole and bends their paths; this page is the quantitative orbit theory: the effective potential, the ISCO and Mercury's precession.

title: Solitons
interaction: Launch a hump on a shallow channel governed by the Korteweg-de Vries equation: dispersion alone spreads it, nonlinearity alone steepens it, and together they make a pulse that keeps its shape, taller ones moving faster. Fire a tall soliton through a short one and they pass through each other unchanged except for a shift; start from a cosine and watch it break into a train that later recombines, as in Zabusky and Kruskal's 1965 computation.
takeaway: When nonlinear steepening exactly balances dispersive spreading, a wave can travel without changing shape and survive collisions like a particle.
pitfall: A soliton is not just a lone wave: the defining test is surviving a collision with another, and the page must show it.
why: MAGIC021 'Nonlinear Waves', the UK graduate mathematics course: FPUT, Zabusky-Kruskal, derivation of KdV, solitons and cnoidal waves: https://maths-magic.ac.uk/courses/2020-2021/magic021
overlapWith: waves-interference: linear waves pass through each other and add; this page is the nonlinear case where the wave's height changes its speed.

title: Spin & the Stern-Gerlach experiment
interaction: Chain Stern-Gerlach analyzers at chosen angles and send silver atoms through one at a time: each analyzer splits the beam into exactly two spots, never a smear. Block one output, rotate the next analyzer and watch the counts follow the cosine squared of half the angle; recombine both paths before the next analyzer and the original state is restored.
takeaway: A spin measurement along any axis gives only two answers, and measuring along one axis erases what was known about another.
pitfall: Spin is not the atom spinning: a classical magnet would smear into a band, and the two-spot result is what the page must reproduce.
why: PhET's quantum collection includes a Stern-Gerlach Experiment simulation (ComPADRE record), and MIT 8.05 opens spin with Feynman vol. III ch. 5: https://www.compadre.org/Quantum/items/detail.cfm?ID=7461
overlapWith: quantum-computing: rotates a qubit on the Bloch sphere; this page is the physical experiment that made the qubit's two-valuedness visible.

title: Superconductivity
interaction: Cool a metal through its transition and watch three things happen together: the resistance drops to zero, an applied magnetic field is pushed out (the London equation on a grid, with the penetration depth visible at the edge), and the BCS gap opens in the density of states as the page solves the gap equation at each temperature. Then join two superconductors across a thin barrier and drive a current: the junction's phase runs and a voltage appears only above a critical current.
takeaway: Below a critical temperature electrons pair into a single quantum state that carries current without loss and pushes magnetic fields out.
pitfall: A superconductor is not merely a perfect conductor: a perfect conductor would trap a field present before cooling, a superconductor expels it.
why: MIT OCW 6.763 Applied Superconductivity: London equations and perfect diamagnetism, Josephson junctions, the Cooper problem and BCS: https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/6-763-applied-superconductivity-fall-2005/
overlapWith: semiconductors: electrons in bands switched by doping and voltage; this page is the pairing that makes electrons stop scattering altogether.
